title: My Boss Made Me Work Through My Mother's Funeral. Then His Biggest Client Walked Out of a $9 Million Deal (PART 2)

blocks.text: …you finally learned to put yourself first."

The CEO's name was Victoria Chen. In 1997, her father was dying of cancer in a hospice in Chicago. Victoria was twenty-six, working eighty-hour weeks at her first startup, and terrified she'd lose everything if she took time off. She visited her father for ten minutes at a time between meetings.

"One night she sat me down in the hallway at 2 a.m.," Victoria said. "She said, 'Your company will survive a week without you. Your father won't.' I told her I couldn't afford it. She said, 'You can't afford not to.'"
Victoria took a week off. She was with her father when he died.

She said it was the most important week of her life, and that she built her entire company around what my mother told her: every employee at her firm gets two weeks of paid family leave, no questions asked.

She'd kept in touch with my mother for twenty-nine years. Christmas cards, the occasional lunch. My mother never mentioned it to me. She saw Victoria's company name on my work calendar a few months before she died and told Victoria, "If my daughter ever forgets herself, give her my letter."
Victoria had come to the funeral to pay her respects. She only realized who I was when she saw my face in the front pew, still in my work clothes, with my laptop bag at my feet.
The envelope held a letter in my mother's handwriting: "My sweet girl. You've always worked too hard and apologized too much.
If someone ever asks you to choose between your job and the people you love, choose the people. Jobs can be replaced. Mothers can't. P.S. Victoria is a good egg. Let her help you."
I laughed and cried at the same time. Only my mother would call a CEO "a good egg."

Victoria cancelled the $9 million contract that afternoon. She told my former agency's partners exactly why. Within a week, they'd removed my boss from leadership and offered me my job back with severance for the days I'd missed. I declined.

Victoria offered me a position as an executive assistant at her company. I start Monday. The first thing HR handed me was the family leave policy. At the top, in bold, it said: "Your company will survive a week without you."
I didn't tell them where that line came from. Victoria did, at my first staff meeting. Then she asked everyone to call their mothers that week.
